questions.question: What are the ACID properties of a database transaction?
questions.title: ACID Properties of Database Transactions
questions.direct_answer: ACID names four transaction properties. Atomicity gives an all-or-nothing outcome. Consistency means successful work preserves the rules the schema and application actually enforce. Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe, with strength depending on the isolation level. Durability means an acknowledged commit survives recovery within the configured storage guarantees.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what each ACID property means in practice and can explain why each matters with concrete examples.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing the four-letter acronym without understanding scenarios where each property prevents data corruption or loss.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: ACID does not invent business rules or make every transaction serial; constraints, isolation, concurrency control, and durability settings define the real guarantee.

sections.title: What ACID Properties Guarantee in Database Transactions
sections.content:
**Atomicity** means all changes in a transaction commit or none do. **Consistency** means a successful transaction preserves the constraints and business rules that are actually encoded. **Isolation** controls what concurrent transactions can see and how conflicts are handled; the selected isolation level matters. **Durability** means an acknowledged commit can be recovered after a restart within the database and storage configuration.

For a bank transfer, atomicity keeps the debit and credit together. A balance rule still has to be implemented with a constraint or correct application logic. Concurrent withdrawals may require a lock, version, conditional update, or stronger isolation. Durability then protects the committed result according to the selected database settings.

sections.title: ACID at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Atomicity|~All or nothing|all changes commit or none|rollback the unit|debit and credit together
blue|Consistency|~Preserve enforced rules|constraints plus correct logic|a missing rule is not invented|balance rule must be encoded
emerald|Isolation|~Concurrent visibility and conflicts|strength depends on the level|locks or versions may be needed|not automatic serial execution
violet|Durability|~Recover an acknowledged commit|within configured guarantees|often uses WAL or redo|replicas and backups cover other failures

sections.title: Spring Transaction with ACID Properties in Action
The Same Transaction in Raw SQL (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT)
sections.content:
```sql
-- A money transfer as one atomic unit of work.
BEGIN;                                          -- start the transaction

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100
 WHERE id = 1;                                  -- debit the sender

SAVEPOINT after_debit;                           -- optional checkpoint

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100
 WHERE id = 2;                                  -- credit the receiver

-- If the credit looked wrong, undo just that step:
--   ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_debit;

COMMIT;                                          -- make both changes permanent

-- If anything had failed before COMMIT, we would run:
--   ROLLBACK;   -- the database stays exactly as it was before BEGIN
```

*Everything between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` is one all-or-nothing unit. `SAVEPOINT` lets you undo part of the work without abandoning the whole transaction.*

sections.title: Why Atomicity Needs an Explicit Boundary
sections.content:
A statement executed by a transactional database is normally atomic, but several statements do not automatically form one unit. In autocommit mode, a successful statement can commit before the next one starts. If a debit commits and the process stops before the credit, the business operation is incomplete.

An explicit transaction groups changes made through the same transactional resource so they commit or roll back as one unit. It does not automatically include a remote API, message broker, or non-transactional storage engine.

sections.title: Without a transaction — a crash leaves money missing
sections.content:
```sql
-- With autocommit enabled and no explicit transaction,
-- each successful UPDATE commits on its own.
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
-- *** application stops here ***
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;  -- never runs

-- Result: the debit committed without the matching credit.
```

sections.title: Wrapped in one transaction — all or nothing
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;  -- not yet committed
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;  -- not yet committed
COMMIT;                                                     -- commit both changes
```

*If the work is rolled back before a successful commit, neither balance change persists. In Spring's usual proxy mode, `@Transactional` declares a similar boundary; its propagation and rollback rules still determine the exact behavior.*

sections.title: When You Need ACID Transaction Guarantees
sections.content: Use a transaction when changes on the same transactional resource must commit or roll back together, or when a read needs a defined snapshot, lock, or isolation level. A transfer's debit and credit are a clear atomic unit. Order creation and stock reservation may share a transaction when they use the same database, but preventing overselling still requires a conditional update, lock, version, or suitable isolation rule. Remote payment or messaging normally needs idempotency and a recovery pattern such as an outbox or saga rather than one local database transaction.

sections.title: Common Mistakes Freshers Make with ACID
sections.content:
- **Assuming repository calls form one unit automatically**: Without an outer transaction, repository methods can complete in separate transactions, so related multi-step work may not be atomic.
- **Treating isolation as perfect separation**: A named level allows particular behaviors, and database implementations differ. Stronger isolation can block or abort work and may require retries; its cost is workload-specific.
- **Treating durability as a backup**: Durability covers an acknowledged commit within configured storage guarantees. Replication, backups, and recovery procedures cover other failures such as media loss or accidental deletion.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Atomicity**: All operations in a transaction succeed or all fail — no partial updates leave data inconsistent
**Consistency**: Successful work preserves the constraints and business rules that are actually encoded
**Isolation**: Controls concurrent visibility and conflicts; the selected level and engine behavior matter
**Durability**: An acknowledged commit survives recovery within the configured storage guarantees
**Spring boundary**: `@Transactional` delegates to a transaction manager; it does not create missing constraints or stronger database guarantees

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: ACID names four transaction properties. Atomicity means all changes commit or none do. Consistency means successful work preserves the rules that the schema and application actually enforce. Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe, and the selected isolation level determines its strength. Durability means an acknowledged commit can be recovered after a restart within the configured storage guarantees. In a bank transfer, debit and credit belong to one atomic transaction. A balance rule must still be encoded, concurrent withdrawals may need a lock or conditional update, and the durability configuration protects the committed result. In Spring, `@Transactional` declares the boundary and delegates to a transaction manager; by default, a `RuntimeException` or `Error` causes rollback while checked exceptions need an explicit rollback rule.

questions.question: How does Spring's @Transactional annotation work?
questions.title: How @Transactional Works in Spring
questions.direct_answer: `@Transactional` declares a transaction boundary. With the usual proxy-based setup, Spring intercepts a call through the bean proxy, asks the configured transaction manager to begin or join a transaction, runs the method, and then commits or rolls back. By default, `RuntimeException` and `Error` cause rollback; checked exceptions do not unless the rollback rules are changed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the transaction boundary, rollback rules, propagation, and the difference between a call through a Spring proxy and self-invocation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming an inner `@Transactional` annotation is applied during self-invocation. In proxy mode the inner call is not intercepted, although an outer transaction may already be active.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that method visibility depends on proxy type and Spring version: private methods cannot be intercepted, while class-based proxies can support protected or package-visible methods in current Spring versions.

sections.title: How Spring's @Transactional Annotation Manages Database Transactions
sections.content:
Spring's **`@Transactional` annotation** declares a transaction boundary. In the common proxy-based mode, a call through the Spring bean proxy is intercepted. The proxy asks a `PlatformTransactionManager` to begin a new transaction or join an existing one according to propagation, runs the method, and then completes the transaction.

A normal return normally leads to commit. By default, `RuntimeException` and `Error` mark the transaction for rollback; a checked exception does not unless `rollbackFor` or another rollback rule says so. Commit itself can still fail, for example when the database checks a deferred constraint. A direct call from one method to another on the same object does not pass through the proxy, so the inner annotation is not applied.

sections.title: The @Transactional Commit Lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Caller invokes method through Spring proxy] --> B[Transaction manager begins or joins a transaction]
    B --> C[Method and resource operations run]
    C --> D{Outcome and rollback rules}
    D -->|normal return| E[Attempt commit]
    D -->|RuntimeException or Error| F[Roll back by default]
    D -->|checked exception| G[Commit by default unless a rollback rule matches]
    E --> H[Complete and release resources]
    F --> H
    G --> H
```

*Propagation and rollback rules can change this flow, and a commit attempt can itself fail.*

sections.title: Using @Transactional in a Spring Service
Without @Transactional — the second write can orphan the first
With @Transactional — both writes share one boundary
When to Apply @Transactional Annotation
sections.content:
Use **`@Transactional` around a service operation** when several database changes form one unit, such as saving an order and reducing inventory in the same database. It is also useful when a read needs a consistent transaction view, a lock, or a cursor that remains open.

`readOnly = true` expresses intent and may let a transaction manager or persistence provider optimize, but it is a hint rather than a portable guarantee or a write blocker. Spring Data repository methods have their own transaction settings, yet a service transaction is still needed to group several calls. In proxy mode, call the method through a Spring-managed proxy. Private methods cannot be intercepted; support for other non-public methods depends on proxy type and version.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with @Transactional
sections.content:
- **Misreading self-invocation**: A same-object call bypasses the proxy, so the inner annotation is ignored. An outer transaction may still be active; the mistake is claiming that no transaction can exist at all.
- **Using a private method**: A proxy cannot intercept a private method. Current class-based proxies can support protected or package-visible methods, while interface-based proxies require calls through the interface's public methods.
- **Assuming every exception rolls back**: By default, `RuntimeException` and `Error` cause rollback. Configure `rollbackFor` when a checked exception should roll back.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Proxy-based**: Spring creates a proxy around your bean that intercepts method calls to manage transactions
**Lifecycle**: The transaction manager begins or joins a transaction and applies the configured commit and rollback rules
**Self-invocation caveat**: A same-object call bypasses the proxy, so the inner annotation is not applied
**Visibility depends on proxy type**: Private methods cannot be intercepted; current class-based proxies can support protected and package-visible methods
**Read-only is a hint**: `readOnly = true` communicates intent but is not a portable write prohibition or guaranteed speed-up

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `@Transactional` declares that a Spring-managed operation should run inside a transaction. In the usual proxy-based setup, the proxy asks the configured transaction manager to begin a new transaction or join one, calls the method, and then commits or rolls back. By default, `RuntimeException` and `Error` cause rollback; checked exceptions need an explicit rollback rule when that is the desired behavior. A service method that saves an order and updates inventory is a good boundary because both database changes must agree. Self-invocation does not apply the inner annotation because the call misses the proxy, although an outer transaction may already exist. Private methods cannot be proxied, and support for other non-public methods depends on proxy type. `readOnly = true` is an intent hint, not a guaranteed optimization or write lockout.

questions.question: In practice, when do you actually need a database transaction?
questions.title: When Do You Need a Database Transaction?
questions.direct_answer: Use an explicit transaction when several database operations must commit or roll back as one unit, or when reads need a defined isolation level, lock, or consistent snapshot. One SQL statement is transactional too, but application code may not need to open a wider boundary for an independent statement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment — knowing when to use transactions versus when a single operation doesn't need explicit transaction management.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Choosing a boundary from the number of repository calls alone instead of the atomicity, snapshot, locking, and resource requirements.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name specific real-world scenarios: order creation with inventory updates, money transfers, user registration with email verification records — and explain why each requires a transaction.

sections.title: Deciding When Database Transactions Are Necessary
sections.content:
Use an explicit transaction when changes on the same transactional resource must commit or roll back as one unit. Also use one when a read needs a consistent snapshot, a database lock, or a chosen isolation level. The real question is not how many repository calls appear in the method; it is what outcome must remain true if a failure or concurrent request occurs.

One independent statement is already run transactionally by a transactional database, so it may not need a wider application boundary. Several independent writes do not need to be forced into one unit merely because there are several. Conversely, one read-modify-write workflow may need a boundary plus a lock, version check, or conditional SQL.

sections.title: When You Actually Need a Transaction
sections.content:
amber|Multiple database writes|~Rows must agree|order + line items|all or nothing|classic transaction
blue|External systems|~A database transaction cannot atomically include every remote API|use idempotency or an outbox/saga|plan retries|do not hold locks during slow calls
emerald|Read-modify-write|~A transaction alone may not stop lost updates|choose isolation, locks, version checks, or conditional SQL|test concurrency|make the rule explicit
violet|Independent statement|~The database still runs it transactionally|a wider application boundary may add no value|reads may still need snapshots or locks|decide from semantics

sections.title: Wrapping a Multi-Step Operation
Step 1: Identify Multi-Step Operations Requiring Atomicity
sections.content: Start with the invariant and resource boundary. If an order row, line items, and a conditional stock update live in one database and must agree, one transaction is appropriate. A debit and credit in the same ledger can also share a transaction. A remote email, payment provider, or separate service normally cannot join that local transaction; use an idempotent operation and a recoverable workflow instead. Reads may still need a transaction for repeatable visibility, pessimistic locking, or a cursor even when no row is written.

sections.title: Step 2: Evaluate the Cost of Inconsistency
sections.content:
Ask what happens if the operation partially succeeds. Several writes in the **same transactional database** can share one transaction. A remote card charge and a local order row usually cannot: use idempotency, an outbox, compensation, or a saga so retries are safe.

Also consider concurrency. A transaction does not by itself prevent every lost update or oversell. Choose a suitable isolation level, row lock, optimistic version check, or conditional update such as `UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= ?`, then verify the affected-row count.

sections.title: Common Mistakes Deciding When to Use Transactions
sections.content:
- **Making the boundary too wide**: Holding a database transaction open across slow network calls increases lock time and connection use.
- **Making the boundary too narrow**: Separate repository calls can commit independently when the business operation needs one unit.
- **Assuming `readOnly = true` is mandatory**: It is an intent hint whose effect depends on the transaction manager and provider. Use it deliberately, not as a universal performance rule.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Atomic unit**: Use a transaction when related operations on the participating resource must succeed or fail together
**Independent statements**: The database runs a statement transactionally; the application may not need a wider explicit boundary
**External payment calls**: A local database transaction cannot usually make a remote charge atomic; add idempotency and a recovery workflow
**Inventory management**: Coordinate order and stock writes, and use suitable locking, isolation, versioning, or conditional updates for concurrency
**Resource boundary**: Related changes can share one transaction only when their resources participate in it; remote systems need a recoverable workflow

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Use a database transaction when several operations on the same transactional resource must commit or roll back together. Saving an order, its line items, and a stock change in one database is a clear example. Transactions also matter for reads that need a consistent snapshot, a lock, or a defined isolation level. One independent SQL statement is already transactional, so application code may not need a wider boundary. Concurrency still needs a specific control: isolation, a row lock, optimistic versioning, or a conditional update. A remote payment API cannot normally join the local database transaction, so use idempotency and a recovery pattern such as an outbox or saga. Keep the boundary around the database work and avoid holding it open during slow network calls.

questions.question: What are the four database transaction isolation levels and what read anomalies do they prevent?
questions.title: Transaction Isolation Levels Explained
questions.direct_answer: SQL names four isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE. They set minimum rules for concurrent visibility, but databases can implement stronger behavior. SERIALIZABLE produces an outcome equivalent to some serial order and may abort work that the application must retry.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the trade-off between consistency and performance in concurrent database access and can explain what anomalies each level prevents.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing one anomaly table as universal even though PostgreSQL and InnoDB implement some levels more strongly than the SQL minimum.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain PostgreSQL's READ COMMITTED default and stronger REPEATABLE READ snapshot, InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ default, and the need to retry serialization failures.

sections.title: Understanding Database Isolation Levels and Read Anomalies
sections.content:
Transaction **isolation levels** control what concurrent work can observe and how effects combine. SQL names READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE through a set of prohibited phenomena. These are minimum requirements, not one universal implementation table.

PostgreSQL maps READ UNCOMMITTED to READ COMMITTED and its REPEATABLE READ snapshot also prevents the standard phantom-read example. InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ and combines MVCC consistent reads with next-key locking for locking reads. SERIALIZABLE means the result is equivalent to some serial order; an engine may block or abort a transaction rather than literally run one at a time.

sections.title: Isolation Levels and Anomalies
sections.content:
amber|READ UNCOMMITTED|~Standard permits dirty reads|some engines make it stronger|PostgreSQL maps it up|check the product
blue|READ COMMITTED|~No dirty reads|later statement may see newer commits|PostgreSQL default|statement snapshots there
emerald|REPEATABLE READ|~No non-repeatable reads by standard|phantom behavior varies|InnoDB default|PostgreSQL is stronger than the minimum
violet|SERIALIZABLE|~Equivalent to a serial outcome|may block or abort|retry failures|not always implemented with heavy locks

sections.title: Choosing an Isolation Level
Step 1: Understand the Three Read Anomalies
sections.content: **Dirty reads** happen when you read uncommitted data from another transaction that might roll back — your data is based on changes that never actually happened. **Non-repeatable reads** occur when you read the same row twice in your transaction and get different values because another transaction modified and committed it in between. **Phantom reads** are when you run the same query twice and see different rows because another transaction inserted or deleted rows matching your criteria. Understanding these anomalies is the foundation for choosing isolation levels — each level prevents a different subset of these problems.

sections.title: Step 2: Match Isolation Level to Anomaly Prevention Needs
sections.content: The SQL standard permits dirty reads at READ UNCOMMITTED, forbids them at READ COMMITTED, forbids non-repeatable reads at REPEATABLE READ, and requires a serial outcome at SERIALIZABLE. A product may provide more protection. Choose from the actual invariant and documented engine behavior; financial correctness may also require constraints, row locks, optimistic versions, or conditional writes rather than a level name alone.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with Isolation Levels
sections.content:
- **Using one universal anomaly table**: Same-named levels can be stronger in a specific database.
- **Ignoring retries**: Serializable implementations may abort a transaction with a serialization failure; the application must retry the whole unit safely.
- **Assuming stronger means more locks**: MVCC engines can provide snapshots and detect conflicts without locking every read. Measure the actual workload.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **READ UNCOMMITTED**: The standard permits dirty reads, though some databases map it to a stronger level
**READ COMMITTED**: Prevents dirty reads and is the default in PostgreSQL and Oracle; suitability depends on the invariant and workload
**REPEATABLE READ**: Forbids non-repeatable reads by standard; phantom and snapshot behavior depend on the product
**SERIALIZABLE**: Produces a result equivalent to serial execution and may require retries
**Trade-off principle**: Higher isolation equals better consistency but worse performance and concurrency

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The four SQL isolation levels are READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE. A dirty read sees uncommitted work, a non-repeatable read sees a row change between reads, and a phantom changes the rows matching a repeated predicate. The standard defines minimum protections, but products differ. PostgreSQL maps READ UNCOMMITTED to READ COMMITTED and its REPEATABLE READ snapshot prevents the standard phantom example. InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ and uses both MVCC and locking rules. SERIALIZABLE requires a result equivalent to some serial order and can abort work, so safe retry logic is essential. Choose from the business invariant and the selected database's documentation, not a memorized universal table.

questions.question: What is transaction propagation in Spring and what is the difference between REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW?
questions.title: Spring Transaction Propagation: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW
questions.direct_answer: Transaction propagation defines how a transactional method relates to an existing transaction. REQUIRED, the default, joins one or starts one. REQUIRES_NEW uses a separate physical transaction and suspends the current one when the transaction manager supports suspension; its commit is not undone by a later outer rollback, though an uncaught inner exception can still make the outer method fail.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of transaction propagation — shows you know that at-Transactional has behavior beyond just wrapping a method in begin/commit/rollback.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that REQUIRED is the default, or thinking every at-Transactional always creates a new transaction regardless of context.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a use case for REQUIRES_NEW: audit logging that should be committed even if the main transaction rolls back, or processing individual batch items independently.

sections.title: How Transaction Propagation Controls Nested Transaction Behavior
sections.content:
**Transaction propagation** determines how an annotated call relates to an existing transaction. **REQUIRED** (the default) joins the current transaction or starts one when none exists. **REQUIRES_NEW** uses a separate physical transaction and suspends the current one when the transaction manager supports suspension.

The inner commit is not undone by a later outer rollback. That does not make the calls logically unrelated: an exception from the inner method can still propagate and fail the outer method unless handled, and a database-backed REQUIRES_NEW normally needs another connection while the outer transaction keeps its resources.

sections.title: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW
sections.content:
amber|REQUIRED|~The default|join the caller's transaction|or start one if none|one shared unit
blue|Shared outcome|~Inner work joins outer commit|rollback-only can affect the whole unit|caller may receive UnexpectedRollbackException|one boundary
emerald|REQUIRES_NEW|~Separate physical transaction|suspends outer when supported|commits independently|inner exception can still propagate
violet|Operational cost|~Usually another connection|outer resources stay held|avoid remote notifications inside it|use only for truly independent database work

sections.title: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW

rows: Rolls back only its own transaction

sections.title: When to Use Each Propagation Type
sections.content:
Use **REQUIRED** for related database work such as an order row and its line items. Do not assume a remote email or payment call joins that database transaction.

Use **REQUIRES_NEW** only for database work with a genuinely independent outcome, such as an audit-attempt record that does not reference uncommitted outer data. Plan for another connection, outer locks remaining held, exception propagation, and the possibility that the inner transaction cannot see the outer transaction's uncommitted rows.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with Transaction Propagation
sections.content:
- **Not knowing REQUIRED is the default**: Freshers think every at-Transactional starts a new transaction, but by default methods join existing transactions, which is usually what you want.
- **Overusing REQUIRES_NEW**: Creating independent transactions everywhere breaks atomicity — if orderService calls inventoryService with REQUIRES_NEW, the inventory update commits even if the order creation fails.
- **Ignoring self-invocation**: Propagation only applies when Spring's proxy intercepts the call — calling a REQUIRES_NEW method from within the same class doesn't create a new transaction.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **REQUIRED default**: Most methods use REQUIRED propagation, joining the existing transaction or creating one if needed
**REQUIRES_NEW independence**: Uses a separate physical transaction and suspends the current one when supported
**Audit logging pattern**: Can preserve an independent attempt record, but it must not depend on uncommitted outer rows
**Batch processing use case**: Process individual items in REQUIRES_NEW so one failure doesn't roll back all items
**Rollback scope difference**: REQUIRED shares rollback with outer transaction, REQUIRES_NEW isolates its rollback

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Propagation controls how an annotated call relates to an existing transaction. REQUIRED is the default: it joins the current transaction or starts one. REQUIRES_NEW uses a separate physical transaction and suspends the outer one when the manager supports that operation. Its committed data is not undone by a later outer rollback, but an uncaught inner exception can still fail the outer method. A separate database transaction usually needs another connection and cannot see the outer transaction's uncommitted rows. That makes REQUIRES_NEW suitable only for truly independent work, such as a standalone audit-attempt record. In proxy mode, self-invocation skips the inner propagation setting.

followup_questions: What happens to the outer transaction if REQUIRES_NEW inner transaction fails?

speakable_v2.hook: Propagation decides if a nested call joins your transaction or spins up its own.

beats.text: Propagation is what a transactional method does when it's called inside another transaction. REQUIRED is the default. REQUIRES_NEW is the main alternative. They differ in whether the inner work shares the outer's fate.

items: Pick REQUIRED for work that belongs together. Publishing a post and bumping the author's count should share one transaction.
Pick REQUIRES_NEW when the inner work must survive on its own. Audit logging a failed attempt is the classic case.

beats.text: Say publishing a post fails and rolls back. If the audit log used REQUIRES_NEW, that record still commits. So you keep a trail of the attempt. The gotcha: a self-call skips the proxy, so propagation won't even apply.

speakable_v2.cap: Use REQUIRED for one business unit; use REQUIRES_NEW only when a separate database outcome and its resource cost are intentional.
